title: Patrol Triangle
protagonist: Derek Osei, patrol-sector lead ranger, Kerio Plains Reserve
primary_metric: minutes of ranger travel time to reach a reported incident location, per square kilometer of reserve actually inside a triangle a patrol covers that day

options.A: Recommend the Perimeter Loop -- long, narrow scalene-triangle patrol sectors hugging the reserve's boundary fence
options.B: Recommend the Interior Web -- a denser mesh of near-equilateral triangular sectors radiating from three fixed outposts

scenario_constructions: Derek Osei and Kerio Plains Reserve are fictional, invented for this case -- consistent with the corpus convention used for e.g. Rosa Delgado / the Fermenter case and Dana Okafor / Turbine Channel.

The dry season's remaining length (Overview) is set to four days -- a scenario detail with no real citable source, disclosed as texture rather than sourced externally; the student never computes with it.

Kerio Plains Reserve is explicitly modeled on a real East African rhino conservancy's real published total area, patrol-team density, and workforce scale (S1, S2, S4) -- the fictional reserve name, protagonist, and exact patrol-sector geometry are invented, but the scale-setting figures are real, cited data.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The Perimeter Loop's standard sector side lengths
modeling_assumptions.basis: No real reserve publishes the exact vertex coordinates of a boundary patrol sector. Chosen as a valid triangle (9 + 11 = 20 > 18, satisfying the Triangle Inequality Theorem) at a scale consistent with a boundary-hugging sector on a real 360 km^2 reserve (S1), and deliberately shaped to be unambiguously scalene and obtuse for teaching purposes.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The most dilemma-relevant assumption in the case. The 18 km longest side sets both the sector's area (via Heron's formula) and its worst-case response distance, so the primary-metric ratio for Option A is directly sensitive to it. An earlier draft used a 20 km longest side, which pushed margin_pct just over the SPEC Section 2 20% cap; it was revised down to 18 km specifically to restore balance -- a real tuning step, not incidental.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Number of Perimeter Loop sectors ringing the reserve
modeling_assumptions.basis: Chosen so six sectors at MA1's scale (6 x 38.99 km^2 = 233.9 km^2) form a plausible boundary ring on a 360 km^2 reserve (65% of total area) without claiming more ground than the reserve has.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Changes Option A's total-coverage figure (D2) directly. Does not change the standard-sector ratio (D4), since the primary metric is computed per standard sector, not per total reserve.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The Interior Web's standard sector side length
modeling_assumptions.basis: No real reserve publishes exact interior patrol-triangle dimensions. Chosen so the resulting sector area (14.07 km^2) lands close to the reserve's own real 14 km^2-per-team density standard (S2) -- i.e., close to one team's worth of ground per sector, a deliberate, real-data-grounded design choice rather than an arbitrary number.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The most dilemma-relevant assumption for Option B, symmetric to MA1: this side length sets both the sector's area and its worst-case response distance (which for an equilateral triangle equals exactly one side length from any vertex).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Number of Interior Web sectors radiating from the three outposts, and how they split across the outposts
modeling_assumptions.value_used: 8 total (3 at Outpost 1, 3 at Outpost 2, 2 at Outpost 3)
modeling_assumptions.basis: Chosen so eight sectors at MA3's scale (8 x 14.07 km^2 = 112.5 km^2, 31% of the reserve) leave real, un-patrolled gaps in the reserve's interior -- a genuine, disclosed trade-off consistent with the Interior Web covering less total ground than the Perimeter Loop, not an oversight. The 3/3/2 split is itself deliberate: since each equilateral sector's vertex angle is exactly 60 degrees, six sectors sharing one outpost as their common vertex would close into a complete circle around it -- this case never lets any outpost reach that, so every outpost's own fan of sectors is a genuinely partial wedge, consistent throughout case.md's Background (fixed 2026-09-18 to resolve a real prose contradiction a fresh P7 reader found between a 'bunches of grapes' analogy and a 'radiating fan' description of the same sectors -- see QA_REPORT.md).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Changes Option B's total-coverage figure (D2) directly. Does not change the standard-sector ratio (D4) -- D2's total area is 8 x one sector's area regardless of how the 8 sectors are distributed across the three outposts. This gap is also the load-bearing setup for the case's twist (see FACILITATOR.md).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The three fixed outposts' reported pairwise GPS distances
modeling_assumptions.value_used: Outpost 1-2: 6.0 km, Outpost 2-3: 6.5 km, Outpost 1-3: 13.0 km
modeling_assumptions.basis: A stated scenario data set representing a real, routine field problem: handheld GPS logs recorded on different days by different units do not always agree with each other. Deliberately constructed so 6.0 + 6.5 = 12.5 < 13.0, failing the Triangle Inequality Theorem.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Not a dial meant to be flexed -- this is a constructed geometry-validity check (Challenge D5a), not a source of the primary-metric margin. Its entire purpose is to fail the check and be identified as failing it.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The proposed relay route's east-west and north-south offsets
modeling_assumptions.basis: A stated scenario survey figure for a proposed relay tower site, chosen as a clean right-triangle leg pair (yielding a 10 km hypotenuse) for Challenge D5(b).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Not dilemma-relevant. This deliverable is a standalone geometry check (identifying and using the two legs of a right triangle), independent of the primary metric.

sensitivity_note: SPEC Section 6 applies at a low level: the case's real-world setting (anti-poaching patrol planning) implies a human threat (poachers) off-page. No casualty math is required or implied anywhere in this case -- the entire dilemma is pure coverage geometry. Facilitator note recorded in FACILITATOR.md.

balance.argument_a: The Perimeter Loop covers nearly 2.1x more total reserve area than the Interior Web (233.9 km^2 vs. 112.5 km^2, about 65% vs. 31% of the reserve's real 360 km^2) -- a poaching incident is more likely to occur somewhere inside SOME Perimeter Loop sector simply because it claims so much more of the map, and a faster response to ground that was never patrolled at all is worthless.
balance.argument_b: The Interior Web wins the case's actual primary metric: because its sector is equilateral, no point inside it is ever farther than one side length (5.7 km) from its outpost, giving a 6.84-minute worst-case response time versus the Perimeter Loop's 21.6-minute worst case (set by its 18 km longest side). Dividing each option's time by its own sector area gives 0.4862 min/km^2 for B versus 0.5540 min/km^2 for A -- B is the more efficient plan per square kilometer it actually covers, and needs fewer total patrol teams (16 vs. 18) to be fully staffed.
balance.margin_basis: margin_pct = (ratio_A - ratio_B) / ratio_B x 100, where ratio = response_time_minutes / sector_area_km2 for each option's standard sector, and the denominator is the WINNING option's own ratio (B) -- the same convention used by sensitivity_model.py's efficiency-framed evaluate() (which computes the reciprocal, area/time, and divides by the LOSING/lower efficiency value; both conventions are algebraically identical and both yield 13.95%, so case.json and the mechanical Tier 2 sensitivity sweep never silently disagree). ratio_A = 21.6 / 38.99 (Heron's formula on 18/11/9 km) = 0.5540 min/km^2. ratio_B = 6.84 / 14.07 (equilateral-triangle area formula on side 5.7 km) = 0.4862 min/km^2. Full arithmetic in RESEARCH_LOG.md.
balance.twist_effect: The twist places a confirmed sighting inside Perimeter Loop Sector 4 (one of Option A's six real, disclosed sectors) but outside all eight of Option B's Interior Web sectors -- i.e. inside the 247.5 km^2 (360 - 112.5) of the reserve MA4's own disclosed coverage gap leaves un-patrolled under B. It does not change the computed 13.95% ratio margin or which option wins that ratio -- it invalidates the DIFFERENT, unstated premise that the more efficient option (B) is therefore always the safer recommendation, by producing a concrete incident B's own footprint never reaches at all. A Hero who reverses to A on this evidence is trading a proven 13.95% per-covered-km^2 efficiency edge for coverage of one specific, real gap; a Hero who holds B has to defend leaving that same gap unpatrolled. Neither reversal nor holding position is definitively correct -- see FACILITATOR.md 'Twist' and 'The follow-up is the whole point' for the discussion framing.

deliverables.text: A labeled sector classification table for one standard patrol sector from each option, with every side length listed, classified by side length (scalene or equilateral) and by angle (acute or obtuse), showing the reasoning behind each classification.

An area-and-staffing table: the area of each option's standard sector, the total area each option covers across its stated number of sectors, and the number of patrol teams required per sector using the reserve's real patrol-team density standard.
A response-time table: for each option's standard sector, the travel time in minutes from its outpost to the farthest point in the sector, at the reserve's shared maximum patrol speed.
A primary-metric comparison: for each option, minutes of response time per square kilometer covered, computed from the D2 and D3 results, with the margin between the two options and a recommendation.

An outpost-network geometry check: (a) using the Triangle Inequality Theorem, determine whether the three fixed outposts' reported pairwise distances can actually form a real triangle; (b) for the proposed radio-relay shortcut, label the two legs of the right-triangle route and compute the straight-line distance.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA1's 18 km longest side is a good-faith scenario shape sized to a real 360 km^2 reserve (S1), not a publicly documented real patrol-sector boundary (no reserve publishes exact sector vertex coordinates). sensitivity_model.py's mechanical +/-50% sweep confirms this is genuinely load-bearing: at -50% (9 km) the winner FLIPS from B to A at a 44.3% margin, breaching the SPEC Section 2 20% cap; at +50% the triangle becomes geometrically invalid (27/11/9 km fails the Triangle Inequality Theorem outright), which is itself informative -- the assumption cannot be stretched arbitrarily far in that direction without breaking the shape it describes. Disclosed in full, not softened -- MA1 is the single most fragile, dilemma-relevant assumption in the case.

MA1's 11 km middle side, part of the same scenario-constructed sector shape as side_a_long_km. sensitivity_model.py's sweep shows +50% (16.5 km) flips the winner to A at a 66.3% margin; -50% (5.5 km) makes the triangle geometrically invalid against the other two fixed sides. Load-bearing for the same reason as side_a_long_km -- it participates directly in the Heron's-formula area calculation that sets Option A's ratio.

MA1's 9 km shortest side, part of the same scenario-constructed sector shape. sensitivity_model.py's sweep shows +50% (13.5 km) flips the winner to A at a 66.7% margin; -50% makes the triangle geometrically invalid. Same load-bearing role as the other two Option A sides.

MA3's 5.7 km equilateral side length is a good-faith scenario shape chosen to land near the reserve's real patrol-team density standard (S2, 1 team per 14 km^2), not a publicly documented figure. sensitivity_model.py's sweep shows BOTH directions breach the 20% cap (-50% flips the winner to A at 75.5%; +50% keeps B but widens the margin to 70.9%) -- MA3 is exactly as fragile as MA1's sides, since it sets both Option B's area and its response distance simultaneously. Disclosed in full -- see case.json.modeling_assumptions[MA3] and FACILITATOR.md.

facilitator.twist: A confirmed sighting report lands inside a Perimeter Loop sector but outside every Interior Web sector -- exposing the Interior Web's disclosed interior coverage gaps (MA4) at the exact moment they matter.
facilitator.sensitivity_note: Low-level SPEC Section 6 flag: anti-poaching setting implies an off-page human threat; no casualty math required or implied.
